blocks.text: But there is also another kind of dove's dung among the Arabs, entirely different from this one: namely the very thing commonly called usnen. For it is established that this is called by another name sparrows' dung, or doves' dung. Avicenna, book 2: اشنان [ushnān] [II, 581] الماهية هي انواع الطغها الابيض ويسمي خرو العصافير [al-māhiyya hiya anwāʿ al-ṭghhā al-abyaḍ wa-yusammā khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] What is usnen? It has several species, of which the finest is white, and it is called sparrows' dung. Sylvaticus: Sparrows' dung, usnen. Giggeius: [col. 45] الاشنان [al-ushnān] Alusnen, a cleansing powder, which is called dove's dung. The same elsewhere: الحرض [al-ḥuruḍ] Alhord, usnen, or dove's dung. Likewise: خرو العصافير [khurūʾ al-ʿaṣāfīr] dove's dung, a certain cleansing powder. Likewise: الوشنان [al-wushnān] dove's dung, a kind of medicinal powder. But even so the matter is not settled, since it is not well enough known what usnen properly is. Most hold that it is the same as القلي [al-qilī] alkali, from which a very well-known salt is named. The Pandectarius: The salt alkali is made in this way: Take of the herb otherwise called usnen, etc. The same: Antifilos (read anthyllion) or antili (read anthyllis) in Greek, in Arabic usnen, in Latin salsola, is a herb from which alkali is made. And elsewhere: Usnen, etc. is a herb whose leaves are like those of stonecrop or of the lentil, having a salty taste, from which salt is made. Scaliger against Cardano, Exercitation 104, Section 18: The Arabs call Chali (better kali) the plant which we call Soda. It is a shrub in the province of Narbonne. By grinding and pressing it they produce what they call salicornum, others soda, others alumen catini, from the shape of the basin into which the juice drips, etc. In Serapion it is called usnen. Giggeius: القلي [al-qilī] alkali, etc. or usnen. Golius: اشنان [ushnān] Usnen, the herb alkali, and the ashes made from it, the best and in great quantity in الحوران [al-Ḥawrān] Auranitis, a region of Syria. Likewise: بلس [bils] bils, the same as اشنان [ushnān] usnen. Ashes of alkali. And that Alcanzius, or Alchindus, a most celebrated Arab physician and almost a contemporary of Avicenna, held this opinion, you may gather from the fact that in the chapter On usnen he describes, almost word for word, everything that Avicenna had said about kali, as though usnen and kali did not differ at all. This is partly true, partly false. قلي [qilī] kali, for the Arabs as for the Hebrews, means roasted or fried. So usnen, roasted so that from its ash a kind of lye or soap is made, is rightly called kali. And by this name it is also known to the Hebrews, who write קליא kalia, in the Talmudic tractate Erubim, ch. 3, fol. 28b. In Pomarius קליא is defined as עשב שנשרף ומשימין אפרו בבורית, A kind of herb whose ash, when it is burnt, is put into soap. And in the Aruch: עשב שורפין ונותנין אותו בבורית ורוחצין ידיהם, A herb which they burn and put into soap, in order to wash their hands with it. The Arabs say the very same of their اشنان [ushnān] usnen, or قلي [qilī] ^{(2)}. Thus the verb تاشن [taʾashshana], formed from the noun اشنان [ushnān] usnen, is rendered by the distinguished Golius: He cleansed his hands with ashes of alkali, or with their lye. [II, 582] And Alcamus: غسل يده فيه [ghasala yadahu fīhi] He washed his hand in it, because it is useful للجرب والحكك [li-l-jarab wa-l-ḥakak] for scabies and itching, as is stated in the same place. But as for the view of Sylvaticus, Scaliger, Salmasius on Solinus, and other more recent writers, that this usuen or kali is our soda, or solida ^{(3)}, from which they make glass ^{(4)}, I would not grant it, except for some single species. For the most learned of the Arabs teach that usnen, or kali, is a species in the genus of the chickpea ^{(5)}, which has nothing in common with our soda or solida. Abuchanipha: اجناس الاشنان كثيرة وكلها من الحمص والاشنان الحرض الذي يغسل به الثياب [ajnās al-ushnān kathīra wa-kulluhā min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-ushnān al-ḥuruḍ alladhī yughsalu bihi al-thiyāb] The kinds of usnen are many, [col. 46] all of which are from the chickpeas (if the word may be pardoned), and usnen is alhord, with which garments are washed. [II, 583] In agreement with this is Serapion, chapter 257: Usnen is a very hot herb, whose species are from amoch (read from amos, من حمص [min ḥimmaṣ] from chickpeas) and usnen is haron (read hord حرض [ḥuruḍ]) and it is that with which cloths are washed. Again elsewhere Abuchanipha: القلي يتخذ من الجمص واجوده ما يتخذ من الحرض وهو قلي الصباغين وساير ذلك الزجاجين [al-qilī yuttakhadhu min al-jmṣ wa-ajwaduhu mā yuttakhadhu min al-ḥuruḍ wa-huwa qilī al-ṣabbāghīn wa-sāʾir dhālika al-zajjājīn] Alkali is taken from the chickpea; but the best is that taken from alhord, which is the kali of the dyers, as the rest is that of the glassmakers. Albacra: الاشنان نبات لا ورق له وله اعضان دقاق شبه العقر وهي رخصة كثيرة الما وتعظم حتي يكون له خشب غليظ يتوقد به وناره حر جدا ورايحته ودخانه كريهة وطعمة الي الملوحة وهو من الحمص [al-ushnān nabāt lā waraq lahu wa-lahu aʿḍān diqāq shibh al-ʿqr wa-hiya rakhṣa kathīrat al-māʾ wa-taʿẓumu ḥattā yakūna lahu khashab ghalīẓ yutawaqqadu bihi wa-nāruhu ḥarr jiddan wa-rāʾiḥatuhu wa-dukhānuhu karīha wa-ṭaʿmuhu ilā al-mulūḥa wa-huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ] Usnen is a plant without leaves, having slender branches like a root, tender, full of moisture, which grow until there is dense wood in them, with which fire is kindled, which is very hot. Its smell and smoke are abominable, its taste salty. And it is in the genus of chickpeas. Alcamus: القلي شي يتخذ من حريق الحمص [al-qilī shayʾ yuttakhadhu min ḥarīq al-ḥimmaṣ] Alkali, a thing obtained from the burning of chickpeas. Abenbitar, from Abuchanipha, in the chapter قاقلي [qāqulī] kakeli,: هو من الحمص والناس ياكولونه مع اللبن وهو مثل الاشنان الا ان القلام اعظم منه وورقه شبيه بورق الحرف [huwa min al-ḥimmaṣ wa-l-nās yaʾkulūnahu maʿa al-laban wa-huwa mithl al-ushnān illā anna al-qlām aʿẓam minhu wa-waraquhu shabīh bi-waraq al-ḥurf] It is a species of chickpea, which is eaten with milk, and it is like usnen, except that it has a larger stalk, and a leaf like the leaf of cress. Giggeius: الغولان [al-ghawlān] Algaulano, a kind of chickpea similar to alusnen ^{(6)}. What of the fact that in 2 Sam. XVII, 28. the Hebrew קלי kali is rendered by Jerome fried chickpea? This will seem novel to those who know that the Hebrew kali does not mean chickpea but roasted grain, Levit. XXIII, 14. Ruth. II, 14. 1 Sam. XVII, 17. and XXV, 18. etc. Yet Jerome's version is doubtless correct. For there the Ammonites and Gileadites are said to have brought to David, a fugitive in the desert, wheat, and barley, and flour, וקלי, and kali, and beans, and lentils, וקלי, and kali. So in the same verse the noun kali is repeated twice. The first, joined to wheat, barley and flour, means roasted grain. But the second, which follows beans and lentils, denotes some roasted or fried legume, namely fried chickpea. For the chickpea was customarily fried or roasted.
